headline: Japan now has cooling booths for one person

sources.title: Watch: 'Human refrigerator' debuts in Japan amid rising temperatures
Japan now has human refrigerators inspired by vending machines
Japan creates fridge for humans (video, CBS Chicago)

chunks.text: Japan's newest [[refrigerator]] is built for people. The Do Hiemon Box is a [[booth]] the size of a [[vending machine]]. One person steps inside, and air at 41 degrees Fahrenheit blows onto the head, neck, shoulders and back. After 20 minutes the machine {{shuts itself off}}. One of the first units has gone to Maebashi City Hall in Gunma Prefecture, where anyone can {{drop in}} and use it free during [[opening hours]].

verbs.correct: To stop a machine from working
verbs.wrong: To make a machine work faster
verbs.why: Shut off means to stop a machine from working, either by a person or automatically. This cooling booth shuts itself off after twenty minutes, so nobody has to remember a timer.

verbs.correct: To visit a place without arranging it first
verbs.wrong: To leave something at a place for later
verbs.why: Drop in means to visit a place casually, without an appointment or advance planning. Anyone can drop in at the Maebashi city hall booth during opening hours.

chunks.text: SDRS, which makes refrigeration units and vending machines, modeled the booth on the chilled drink machines found on streets across Japan. Inside, the temperature sits at 59 degrees, with three [[airflow]] settings. The booth is [[on wheels]] and needs no {{setting up}}. It is [[aimed at]] construction sites, factories, warehouses and outdoor events.

verbs.correct: To assemble something ready for use
verbs.wrong: To start a journey to another place
verbs.why: Set up means to prepare something so people can use it, like a tent or a new device. This cooling booth needs no setting up: it arrives ready to use immediately.

chunks.text: Temperatures in Japan have reached [[close to]] 100 degrees [[in recent weeks]], and the country has {{brought in}} a new weather category for the hottest days. In Tokyo, 48 people were taken to the hospital with [[heatstroke]] on July 15. SDRS says people feel [[noticeably]] cooler within about five minutes. The company also says ten minutes inside may [[relieve]] the [[symptoms]] of [[heat exhaustion]]. It adds that the booth uses about half the electricity of a spot air conditioner, the [[portable]] kind used on factory floors. Those are the company's own [[claims]], and it has published no independent testing to {{back them up}}.

verbs.correct: To introduce a new rule or system
verbs.wrong: To mention a subject in conversation
verbs.why: Bring in means to introduce something new, like a rule, a system, or in this case a new weather category for extreme heat. Officials bring in new categories when old ones no longer fit reality.

verbs.correct: To support a claim with evidence
verbs.wrong: To repeat a claim more loudly
verbs.why: Back up means to support a claim with solid evidence, such as data or independent testing. A company's own claims about a product need proof to back them up before we trust them fully.

chunks.text: The standard model costs 1.5 million yen [[plus tax]], about $9,300, and is sold to businesses [[rather than]] households. Trusco Nakayama, an industrial equipment supplier, is {{rolling the booths out}} through [[distributors]] [[nationwide]]. The Maebashi unit came as a [[donation]], so the city offers it free. Whether the idea {{catches on}} [[elsewhere]] is [[not yet clear]]. For the builders and road crews working outdoors, the [[appeal]] is simple. Step inside, {{cool off}} for five minutes, then back to work.

verbs.correct: To make a new product available widely
verbs.wrong: To test a product before using it
verbs.why: Roll out means to make a new product available to more people or places, little by little or all at once. Trusco Nakayama is rolling these cooling booths out through distributors nationwide.

verbs.correct: To become popular with many people
verbs.wrong: To reach the same level as others
verbs.why: Catch on means to become popular and spread to many people over time. It is not yet clear whether these cooling booths will catch on outside of Japan.

verbs.correct: To become cooler after being too hot
verbs.wrong: To blow air onto a person's head
verbs.why: Cool off means to become less hot after being too warm, whether that is a person, a room, or an engine. Workers can step into the booth and cool off for a few minutes.

mainIdea.s: A Japanese company has built a one-person cooling booth to help outdoor workers deal with extreme heat. The company's claims about its cooling power have not been independently tested.
mainIdea.why: SDRS built the Do Hiemon Box for construction sites and outdoor work. It has published no independent testing to back up its claims about cooling power.

mainIdea.s: The government is giving these cooling booths away free to households across Japan to fight the summer heat. Independent tests have confirmed the booths cut heatstroke cases in half.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the standard booth is sold to businesses, not given away to households. Only the company, not independent tests, has made these cooling claims.

mainIdea.s: Several cities in Japan opened public cooling shelters this month for residents during the hottest hours. The shelters are staffed by volunteers and offer free water to every visitor.
mainIdea.why: This story is about public cooling shelters run by cities, not the one-person cooling booth made by the private company SDRS.
